Selective inference for pruned interaction trees
with known unequal variances in randomized trials

Tomoshige Nakamura ††thanks: Faculty of Health Data Science, Juntendo University
1 November 2026
Abstract

Interaction trees reuse outcomes to discover treatment-effect heterogeneity, complicating inference after growth and pruning. We develop selective inference for generalized least-squares (GLS) interaction trees with a common covariate basis and known unequal variances. Under a conditional Gaussian model with positive diagonal covariance, weighted orthogonality reduces survival under additive fixed-penalty pruning to one quadratic inequality supplementing the growth event. This yields exact finite-sample conditional tests and confidence intervals, with retained-path and complete-tree inference agreeing on compatible sections. Under causal identification and a correct reference prognosis, the pruning-invariant GLS target is a signed finite-design weighted contrast of conditional average treatment effects. Simulations at n=100,200,400,800n=100,200,400,800 and maximum depths one to three search all adjacent-observation midpoints, support calibration and demonstrate over-rejection when pruning survival is omitted. Compared with a 50:50 honest procedure, full-data learning improves reference-split recovery in some small-sample settings. Root-level median intervals can be shorter, while deep-node intervals and upper tails can be much wider; these comparisons concern each procedure’s selected targets. Estimating a common scale with the variance ratio fixed produces modest changes in Selective coverage in the settings examined, without extending the exact guarantee. An exploratory ACTG 175 analysis provides a working-model illustration with estimated arm variances.

Keywords: heterogeneous treatment effects; interaction trees; prognostic adjustment; pruning; randomized trials; selective inference.

1 Introduction

Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) establish how treatments compare on average, but clinical decisions also require understanding whether their relative benefits vary across patients. A treatment that is useful overall may be more beneficial for patients with particular combinations of baseline characteristics. Discovering such subgroups can generate hypotheses for subsequent trials and help describe treatment-effect variation (Su et al., 2011; Athey and Imbens, 2016). The relevant question concerns differences between treatment responses: a characteristic that predicts a good outcome under both treatments need not identify patients who benefit more from one treatment than the other.

Interaction trees offer an interpretable approach to this problem. They recursively partition participants using treatment-by-subgroup comparisons, producing baseline rules that describe possible effect modifiers (Su et al., 2009). Their clinical applications include exploration of quality-of-life responses to a psychoeducational programme for breast cancer survivors (Su et al., 2011) and substance-use treatment engagement following motivational interviewing (Steingrimsson and Yang, 2019). An ensemble extension, random forests of interaction trees, has been used to study variation in the response to acupuncture for chronic headache (Su et al., 2018). These applications motivate the subgroup question addressed here; the present theory is developed for a specified single-outcome tree, with longitudinal and ensemble extensions requiring separate arguments.

After a tree has been discovered, an additional question arises: how strong is the statistical evidence for its apparent treatment-effect differences? The same outcomes usually determine the split variables, thresholds, and which branches remain after pruning. An ordinary interaction test at a selected split therefore treats an outcome-dependent choice as if it had been specified in advance. This reuse of outcomes is closely related to the model-selection problem studied in selective inference for the lasso, where inference on selected coefficients accounts for the data-dependent choice of model (Lee et al., 2016). Selective inference for lasso-selected effect modification has also been developed using residualization and asymptotic arguments (Zhao et al., 2022). Existing tree-based work provides inferential tools, including an overall interaction permutation test (Su et al., 2011), bootstrap-calibrated subgroup intervals (Loh et al., 2019), and uncertainty estimates for interaction-tree ensembles (Su et al., 2018). The issue addressed here is more specific: finite-sample conditional tests and confidence intervals for individual retained treatment interactions after growing and pruning a specified deterministic tree on the same data.

Tree-Values provides a route to such inference for regression trees (Neufeld et al., 2022). Building on conditional Gaussian selective inference (Lee et al., 2016), it accounts for the CART selection event when testing response means or contrasts in discovered regions. Under its Gaussian model with known common variance, it controls the conditional type-I error of an individual selected test and provides confidence intervals with conditional coverage. Its theory includes fixed-penalty pruning. The paper also discusses general known-covariance Gaussian conditioning, while noting that the computational reductions need not extend. The Box Lunch Study application, involving a regression analysis of caloric intake with estimated variance, gives a concrete illustration of inference for CART-discovered groups; it is not a treatment-heterogeneity analysis. Extending this approach to treatment interactions requires new structural arguments because their contrasts compare treated and control outcomes within each child region, rather than only comparing child outcome means.

Sample splitting supplies another established route to inference after subgroup discovery. Honest causal trees learn subgroups using one sample and estimate their effects using independent observations (Athey and Imbens, 2016). Independence protects the estimation stage from the outcome-driven search. The allocation of observations to the two stages can nevertheless affect the learned tree, the resulting inferential target, and interval precision. Although the overall analysis uses both parts, each stage has access to only a subset of the responses. This constraint can be consequential when the trial is small, or when recursive splits leave few treated and control participants in a parent region. Using all responses for construction and inference avoids the additional random partition, but requires accounting for selection and need not produce shorter intervals. The trade-off between independent estimation and selective reuse is therefore an empirical question as well as a theoretical one.

We extend the selective-inference strategy of Tree-Values to a covariate-adjusted interaction tree for quantitative RCT outcomes. The tree uses generalized least-squares (GLS) interaction scores, a prespecified prognostic basis common to every node, and additive pruning with a fixed penalty. The Gaussian covariance is known and diagonal, allowing different outcome variances in the treatment arms. Our main contribution is to establish the weighted orthogonality that makes this extension tractable: along the appropriate target-specific perturbation, on a section preserving the grown path, off-path candidates and other selected scores remain fixed. This yields an exact pruning-survival constraint, finite-sample conditional tests and confidence intervals, and a factorization showing that retained-path conditioning and complete-tree conditioning give identical inference on compatible sections. The pruning objective and Gaussian conditioning principle have precedents; the new results concern their validity and computational reduction for these residualized treatment interactions. We also identify the inferential target and its causal interpretation. It is a finite-design GLS interaction coefficient and, under causal identification and a correctly specified reference-treatment prognosis, a signed weighted contrast of conditional average treatment effects. It generally differs from an ordinary subgroup-average-effect difference; within-child homogeneous effects recover the child-to-child difference. Equal outcome variance is an explicit special case.

The experiments assess both the inferential correction and its practical cost at sample sizes n=100,200,400,800n=100,200,400,800 and maximum growth depths one to three. We search all adjacent-observation midpoints and compare naive inference, growth-only selective inference, pruning-aware inference, and a same-rule 50:50 honest procedure. The comparisons distinguish split-level error from tree-level error, and calibration from the ability to form a tree, infer a retained interaction, and achieve useful precision. Stronger pruning exposes the additional correction needed after the growth event. Full-data learning can improve recovery of a reference split in a small sample, while root-level median intervals can be shorter and their upper tails longer than those of the honest comparator. The targets and selected populations generally differ, and neither discovery rates nor interval widths establish a uniform advantage. An additional experiment estimates the common scale while keeping the variance ratio known. An ACTG 175 application in HIV infection compares two combination regimens using original-scale 20-week CD4 counts and an unpruned tree with maximum depth three. Its estimated arm variances, residual tail departures, and public-subset limitations make it a working-model illustration; the exact guarantee requires the stated Gaussian model and known covariance. These restrictions also distinguish the projection-level inference developed here from an unrestricted claim about clinical subgroup benefits.

The remainder of the article is organized as follows. Section 2 introduces the RCT setting, interaction trees, and the outcome-reuse problem. Section 3 presents the proposed selective-inference procedure, including the interaction-tree construction, target contrasts, and selection-adjusted tests and intervals. Section 4 establishes the target properties and selective-inference results. Section 5 reports the simulation design, comparison procedures, and results for small and moderate samples, Section 6 presents the ACTG 175 analysis, and Section 7 discusses limitations and further work. Appendices A and B contain the proofs and additional structural results.

2 Problem setup and interaction trees

2.1 RCT setting and the subgroup question

For participants i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, let Xi∈ℝpX_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} be baseline covariates, Ai∈{0,1}A_{i}\in\{0,1\} the assigned treatment, and YiY_{i} a quantitative outcome. Write Yi​(a)Y_{i}(a) for the potential outcome under treatment aa. The scientific question is whether combinations of baseline characteristics describe variation in the relative treatment response, rather than merely predicting a high or low outcome under either treatment. The scientific target is variation in the conditional average treatment effect (CATE), τ⁡(x)=𝔼⁡{Yi​(1)−Yi​(0)∣Xi=x}\tau(x)=\mathbb{E}\{Y_{i}(1)-Y_{i}(0)\mid X_{i}=x\}. Such variation can motivate interpretable candidate subgroups for further investigation.

For the statistical analysis, condition throughout on the realized design 𝒟=(X,A)\mathcal{D}=(X,A). Fix a known positive diagonal matrix VV, specified conditional on 𝒟\mathcal{D} without using YY. The exact selective-inference results use the following sampling model; randomization alone does not imply it.

Assumption 1 (Gaussian sampling with known diagonal covariance).

Conditional on 𝒟\mathcal{D}, Y∼Nn​(μ,σ2​V)Y\sim N_{n}(\mu,\sigma^{2}V) for arbitrary μ∈ℝn\mu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, known 0<σ2<∞0<\sigma^{2}<\infty, and the known positive diagonal VV above. For arm-specific variances this includes

σ2=σ02,Vi​i=𝟏{Ai=0}+ρ𝟏{Ai=1},ρ=σ12/σ02>0,\sigma^{2}=\sigma_{0}^{2},\qquad V_{ii}=\mathbf{1}\{A_{i}=0\}+\rho\mathbf{1}\{A_{i}=1\},\qquad\rho=\sigma_{1}^{2}/\sigma_{0}^{2}>0, (1)

where both arm variances are known. Conditional independence of outcomes is retained; correlated outcomes are not covered by the local structural results below.

Known variance is also part of the exact Gaussian theory in Tree-Values (Neufeld et al., 2022). Randomization does not imply equality of the two potential-outcome variances. Here it is the known variance shape, rather than equality across arms, that is used in weighted construction and conditioning.

For causal interpretation, let Bi⋅=b(Xi)𝖳B_{i\cdot}=b(X_{i})^{\mathsf{T}} for a fixed finite-dimensional baseline basis b⁡(x)∈ℝqb(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{q} containing an intercept. The same basis, restricted to the participants in a region, will be used at every node, and its specification uses no outcomes. The next assumption separates causal identification in the analyzed sample from the additional restriction on the reference-treatment prognosis. The latter is not supplied by randomization. This assumption is needed for the causal reading of the target defined in Section 3.1, but not for Gaussian inference on that projection target.

Assumption 2 (Causal identification and reference prognosis).

Potential outcomes satisfy consistency and no interference. Conditional on the full covariate design XX, the allocation vector AA is independent of the full potential-outcome vector, and 0<ℙ⁡(Ai=1∣X)<10<\mathbb{P}(A_{i}=1\mid X)<1. For a=0,1a=0,1, suppose 𝔼⁡{Yi​(a)∣X}=ma​(Xi)\mathbb{E}\{Y_{i}(a)\mid X\}=m_{a}(X_{i}) and m0​(x)=b​(x)𝖳​βm_{0}(x)=b(x)^{\mathsf{T}}\beta for an unknown β\beta. Write τ⁡(x)=m1​(x)−m0​(x)\tau(x)=m_{1}(x)-m_{0}(x), so that

μ=B​β+A⊙τX,τX=(τ⁡(X1),…,τ⁡(Xn))𝖳.\mu=B\beta+A\odot\tau_{X},\qquad\tau_{X}=(\tau(X_{1}),\ldots,\tau(X_{n}))^{\mathsf{T}}. (2)

These assumptions concern the analyzed sample. Selection into an available data file is not supplied with an identification guarantee by randomization in an original, larger trial.

Under Assumption 2, m1​(x)−m0​(x)m_{1}(x)-m_{0}(x) agrees with this CATE by iterated expectation. The vector μ\mu is the mean before conditioning on the subsequently selected tree.

2.2 Interaction trees

An interaction tree recursively divides the baseline covariate space to explore treatment-effect variation (Su et al., 2009). The root contains all analyzed participants. At a reached parent region RR, a candidate rule ss, such as a baseline-variable threshold, divides RR into a left child RLR_{L} and a right child RRR_{R}. Repeating this operation produces a sequence of baseline rules for each terminal group.

The distinction from an ordinary outcome-prediction tree is the comparison used to assess a split. To illustrate it, suppose all four treatment-by-child cells are nonempty and write Y¯a,C\bar{Y}_{a,C} for the observed mean in treatment arm aa and child C∈{L,R}C\in\{L,R\}. An unadjusted empirical interaction contrast for a fixed candidate is

Δ^s=(Y¯1,L−Y¯0,L)−(Y¯1,R−Y¯0,R).\widehat{\Delta}_{s}=(\bar{Y}_{1,L}-\bar{Y}_{0,L})-(\bar{Y}_{1,R}-\bar{Y}_{0,R}).

It compares the observed treatment differences across the two children. A split can have little difference between the children’s overall outcome means while exhibiting a large treatment interaction, or conversely. Interaction-tree splitting uses a measure of this interaction, commonly standardized for uncertainty, to compare candidate rules. Covariate-adjusted interaction trees additionally account for prognostic baseline variables (Steingrimsson and Yang, 2019).

This four-cell display explains the interaction principle. It is not the definition of the adjusted GLS score or projection target used in this paper, and conditional on a realized design it is not asserted to be an unbiased estimate of a pure causal subgroup-effect difference. Section 3.1 specifies our common-basis GLS construction.

Growing a tree applies the split comparison recursively within the resulting children. A stopping rule limits further growth, for example through a maximum depth or a minimum number of observations in each treatment-by-child cell. Pruning then collapses branches of a grown tree to obtain a smaller collection of interactions. Interaction-complexity pruning balances the retained split scores against a penalty per retained split (Su et al., 2009; Steingrimsson and Yang, 2019). The specific deterministic growth rule, fixed-penalty objective, and tie convention analyzed here are specified in Section 3.1, under Assumptions 3 and 4; the results do not cover every implementation called an interaction tree.

2.3 Outcome reuse and the inferential problem

The observed outcomes enter both stages of this search: they determine which candidate rule wins at each reached node and which grown splits survive pruning. An interaction selected for having a large score is therefore not a prespecified contrast. The ordinary reference distribution for testing a fixed interaction does not automatically remain appropriate after selecting it from competing rules. Even when the numerical pruning penalty is fixed in advance, the event that a particular branch survives still depends on the outcomes.

The question in this paper is how to test and form a confidence interval for the interaction at a prespecified node address when it is retained, using the same responses for tree construction and inference. A collapsed or ungrown address has no split-specific inferential result to report. The target is the adjusted treatment-by-child projection defined in Section 3.1; its causal interpretation and distinction from an ordinary subgroup-average-effect difference are established in Section 4.1. The reporting goal is individual selected-split inference. A guarantee for every retained split separately is not, by itself, a familywise guarantee for the whole tree.

Tree-Values addresses outcome reuse for CART response-mean targets by conditioning on selection (Neufeld et al., 2022). We use the same selective-inference strategy for the specified interaction tree. Section 3 defines the procedure, and Section 4 derives the restrictions imposed by growth and pruning and the resulting conditional law. Those restrictions, rather than an ordinary fixed-contrast reference distribution, determine the test and confidence interval.

3 Proposed selective inference procedure

The proposed method uses all observed responses to construct the specified interaction tree and to perform inference on one retained treatment interaction. Its inputs are the observed design and outcomes, an outcome-independent common basis and growth rules, maximum depth, known σ\sigma and VV, fixed penalty λ\lambda, a prespecified node address, null value θ0\theta_{0}, and level α\alpha. If that address is grown and retained, the output is its original GLS point estimate, a selection-adjusted two-sided pp-value, and a 1−α1-\alpha confidence interval. Otherwise the output is unavailable.

The procedure has three stages: identify the selected split and its original interaction contrast; compute all statistic values that reproduce its ancestral growth choices and survival after pruning; and use the Gaussian distribution restricted to that set for testing and interval inversion. It retains the same point estimate as the full-data naive procedure, while changing the reference distribution to account for selection. Section 3.1 specifies the tree and contrasts; Section 3.2 gives the proposed inference. Section 4 establishes its conditional guarantees.

Deterministic growth.

Assumption 3 (Finite deterministic local growth).

Fix a finite maximum depth DD, with the root at depth zero. At each reached region of depth less than DD, a finite ordered candidate set, eligibility, and stopping rules depend only on 𝒟\mathcal{D} and the region. Each eligible node is split by maximizing Gs​(y)G_{s}(y). Candidates with identical matrices ℓs​ℓs𝖳\ell_{s}\ell_{s}^{\mathsf{T}} are represented by the first in the fixed priority order, retaining its geometric split. Other ties use that same order. A node at depth DD or with no eligible candidates is terminal. There is no outcome-dependent stopping, basis selection, or pruning during this growth stage.

The result H^​(y)\widehat{H}(y) is a complete labeled tree: its labels include split variables, thresholds, and child directions, and not merely topology. Every node uses the common basis in Section 2.

A design-feasible labeled grown tree obeys these eligibility and stopping rules with eligible prescribed split labels. This term does not assert that its score-winning event has positive probability. It also covers the forced completions defined below.

Fixed-penalty pruning.

A rooted pruned subtree P⪯HP\preceq H is obtained only by collapsing some internal nodes and all their descendants into terminal nodes. Equivalently, I⁡(P)I(P) is an ancestor-closed subset of I⁡(H)I(H). The root-only tree, with I⁡(P)=∅I(P)=\varnothing, is allowed. Retaining a split retains both immediate child regions, which can themselves be terminal.

Assumption 4 (Additive interaction pruning with collapse at equality).

Fix 0≤λ<∞0\leq\lambda<\infty without using YY. More generally, λ\lambda may be fixed conditional on 𝒟\mathcal{D}, VV, and the known σ\sigma. On the grown tree H=H^​(y)H=\widehat{H}(y), maximize

Qλ​(P,y)=∑w∈I⁡(P)Gw​(y)−λ​|I⁡(P)|,P⪯H.Q_{\lambda}(P;y)=\sum_{w\in I(P)}G_{w}(y)-\lambda|I(P)|,\qquad P\preceq H. (5)

Select the maximizer with the fewest internal nodes by the following explicit recursion. At terminal nodes set FwH​(y)=0F_{w}^{H}(y)=0. At internal nodes set

VwH​(y)=Gw​(y)−λ+FwLH​(y)+FwRH​(y),FwH​(y)=max⁡{0,VwH​(y)}.V_{w}^{H}(y)=G_{w}(y)-\lambda+F_{w_{L}}^{H}(y)+F_{w_{R}}^{H}(y),\qquad F_{w}^{H}(y)=\max\{0,V_{w}^{H}(y)\}. (6)

Starting at the root, retain ww if VwH​(y)>0V_{w}^{H}(y)>0 and then apply the same rule to both children; otherwise collapse ww. In particular, equality is resolved by collapsing. Denote the result by P^λ​(y)\widehat{P}_{\lambda}(y).

No branch is raised or moved. The local contrasts of retained splits are not redefined. The parameter, criterion, and reporting rule are not tuned by the same outcomes.

The penalty in (5) has weighted squared-outcome units for the specified normalization of VV. Using dimensionless scores Gw/σ2G_{w}/\sigma^{2} and a fixed dimensionless penalty λ~\widetilde{\lambda} is equivalent to setting λ=σ2​λ~\lambda=\sigma^{2}\widetilde{\lambda}. Substitution of an estimated σ\sigma is not included in this equivalence under the exact known-variance guarantee.

Proposition 1 (Optimization and exact tie convention).

The recursion in Assumption 4 returns the unique maximizer of (5) having the fewest internal nodes. Its optimal value is FrootH​(y)F_{\rm root}^{H}(y). Once the grown tree and scores are available, this pruning takes a number of arithmetic operations linear in the number of nodes.

Remark 1 (Equal-variance special case).

When V=InV=I_{n}, the definitions in (3) give rs=vsr_{s}=v_{s}, us=ℓs=vs/dsu_{s}=\ell_{s}=v_{s}/d_{s}, and ηs=vs/ds2\eta_{s}=v_{s}/d_{s}^{2}. With the same basis, candidates, stopping rules, priorities, penalty, and known scale, the scores, grown and pruned trees, original targets, and selection sections coincide pointwise with those of the same interaction-tree procedure using unweighted residuals. Consequently its selective pp-values and confidence intervals coincide wherever defined. The comparison is with an unweighted interaction tree, rather than CART response-mean contrasts. In (1), this is ρ=1\rho=1; the common variance σ2\sigma^{2} need not equal one.

3.2 Proposed selective tests and confidence intervals

At a prespecified address that is observed to be retained, record its selected ancestral path γ\gamma and use its original contrast η\eta, with estimate tobs=η𝖳​Yt_{\rm obs}=\eta^{\mathsf{T}}Y and target θ=η𝖳​μ\theta=\eta^{\mathsf{T}}\mu. The known Gaussian reference standard deviation of T=η𝖳​YT=\eta^{\mathsf{T}}Y is ω=σ/d\omega=\sigma/d.

The growth section 𝒯γgrow​(z)\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}^{\rm grow}(z) contains every tt for which the recorded path wins all its target and ancestor comparisons. The proposed procedure uses the further restriction

J⁡(z)=𝒯γgrow​(z)∩{t:d2​t2>δγ​(z)},J(z)=\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}^{\rm grow}(z)\cap\{t:d^{2}t^{2}>\delta_{\gamma}(z)\},

where the second set is the exact pruning-survival gate in (17). Its threshold is computed from the path’s ancestor scores and hanging-subtree pruning values in (13)–(15). The computation includes every component of J⁡(z)J(z). Growth-only inference uses the growth section alone; at positive penalties it can omit restrictions imposed by reporting only pruning survivors. Naive inference instead uses the unrestricted Gaussian reference distribution.

Let Fa,ωJF^{J}_{a,\omega} denote the CDF of N⁡(a,ω2)N(a,\omega^{2}) restricted to JJ, as defined in (19). We evaluate U=Fθ0,ωJ⁡(z)​(tobs)U=F^{J(z)}_{\theta_{0},\omega}(t_{\rm obs}), report p=2​min⁡{U,1−U}p=2\min\{U,1-U\}, and invert this same CDF for the equal-tail confidence interval using (24). Thus the point estimate remains tobst_{\rm obs}, while both the test and interval reflect growth and pruning selection. Theorem 2 gives their individual conditional validity under the stated known-covariance Gaussian model; the causal interpretation requires the additional conditions in Section 4.1. Conditional validity does not guarantee a short interval or simultaneous error control for the whole tree.

Algorithm 1 summarizes the complete procedure for one prespecified address. A collapsed or ungrown address has no split-specific inferential result to report. The procedure retains the original local contrast and does not refit an effect parameter using the final terminal leaves.

Only hanging-subtree values and selected ancestor scores enter δγ​(z)\delta_{\gamma}(z). Their values at YY equal their values at zz, so cached non-target scores can be reused; unconstrained regrowth at zz would generally select a different path and is unnecessary. The growth section for a given path can also be reused across fixed penalties and deeper growth prefixes that preserve the path, while the pruning threshold must be recomputed for each depth and penalty.

The implementation uses S=ℓ𝖳​Y=d​TS=\ell^{\mathsf{T}}Y=dT, with variance σ2\sigma^{2}. Its perturbation direction is b=v/db=v/d, so Y−b​S=ZY-bS=Z and ℓ𝖳​b=1\ell^{\mathsf{T}}b=1. In general b≠ℓb\neq\ell: perturbing along the score loading would give the wrong Gaussian section under unequal variances. On the SS scale, the pruning gate is S2>δγ​(Z)S^{2}>\delta_{\gamma}(Z), and interval endpoints for its mean are divided by dd to obtain the interval for θ\theta. Equivalently, whitening outcomes and all candidate columns gives the unit direction u=V−1/2v/du=V^{-1/2}v/d. At V=InV=I_{n}, b=ℓ=ub=\ell=u and the original implementation is recovered.

All positive-length support components are used in probability calculations. Gaussian masses are evaluated on a log scale using lower-tail or survival probabilities, and mean inversion uses Corollary 1. Floating-point tolerances for near-zero residual norms, slopes, and inversion are distinct from the mathematical exactness statements. The fixed VV and scale σ\sigma are inputs, not variance estimates learned from the analyzed outcomes. Numerical candidate reductions and implementation tolerances are documented in Section B.9 of Appendix B.

4 Theoretical analysis

This section establishes the validity and computational structure of the proposed procedure. We first establish the causal interpretation of the GLS target and its invariance under pruning. We then establish weighted orthogonality, which enables us to derive the exact selection event imposed by tree growth and pruning. These results yield the truncated-Gaussian law and the conditional guarantees for the proposed tests and confidence intervals under the known-covariance Gaussian model. Finally, we show that retained-path and full-tree conditioning give identical inference on compatible sections. Complete proofs are provided in Appendix A.

4.1 Causal interpretation and pruning invariance

Proposition 2 (GLS target, causal interpretation, and pruning invariance).

Under Assumption 2, for each fixed eligible split,

θs=∑i∈IR:Ai=1ηs,iτ(Xi).\theta_{s}=\sum_{i\in I_{R}:A_{i}=1}\eta_{s,i}\tau(X_{i}). (7)

The sums of ηs\eta_{s} in the left-treated, left-control, right-treated, and right-control cells are, respectively, 1,−1,−1,11,-1,-1,1. If τ\tau is constant at τL\tau_{L} and τR\tau_{R} at the realized design points of the two children, then θs=τL−τR\theta_{s}=\tau_{L}-\tau_{R}. In particular, a constant effect on the parent implies θs=0\theta_{s}=0.

Pruning by collapsing descendants leaves this target unchanged for a retained split, provided its original local contrast in (3) is used. Its parent and immediate child partition must not be redefined.

The weights depend on the known variance shape as well as allocation and covariate imbalance, and can be signed. For the same geometric split, the GLS and OLS targets generally differ; both equal τL−τR\tau_{L}-\tau_{R} under the within-child homogeneity in Proposition 2. Thus the target is generally not a difference of ordinary subgroup-average effects. Zero contrast does not imply effect homogeneity. If the reference prognosis is B​β+rB\beta+r instead, the projection target additionally contains ηs𝖳​r\eta_{s}^{\mathsf{T}}r. Gaussian projection coverage then has no automatic interpretation as coverage for a pure treatment-effect contrast. Re-estimation of leaf effects after pruning is a separate inferential problem.

4.2 Weighted orthogonality

Lemma 1 (Weighted descendant orthogonality and orthonormal scores).

For a split ss in region RR, let D′D^{\prime} be one of its children or any region contained in that child. Every candidate rr in D′D^{\prime} satisfies

vs𝖳​W​vr=0,ℓs𝖳​V​ℓr=us𝖳​ur=0.v_{s}^{\mathsf{T}}Wv_{r}=0,\qquad\ell_{s}^{\mathsf{T}}V\ell_{r}=u_{s}^{\mathsf{T}}u_{r}=0. (8)

Contrasts on disjoint parent regions satisfy the same identities. Consequently, for any feasible fixed labeled grown tree HH, its whitened selected vectors {uw:w∈I⁡(H)}\{u_{w}:w\in I(H)\} are orthonormal and orthogonal to V−1/2C0V^{-1/2}C_{0}, where C0=[B,A]C_{0}=[B,A]. For these fixed tree labels, the linear scores Sw=ℓw𝖳​YS_{w}=\ell_{w}^{\mathsf{T}}Y have variance σ2\sigma^{2} and zero pairwise covariance under Assumption 1 before conditioning on tree selection.

Unlike a CART sibling-mean contrast, ℓs\ell_{s} need not be constant within a child. The common-basis restriction argument proves (8) for these adjusted interaction directions. It is this weighted local geometry that permits the section simplification below, rather than a general claim for arbitrary non-diagonal covariance.

4.4 Selective tests and confidence intervals

For a measurable set J⊆ℝJ\subseteq\mathbb{R} with positive Lebesgue measure, define the truncated-normal CDF

Fa,ωJ​(t)=∫J∩(−∞,t]ϕω(w−a)dw∫Jϕω​(w−a)​𝑑w,ϕω​(x)=12​π​ω​exp⁡(−x22​ω2).F^{J}_{a,\omega}(t)=\frac{\displaystyle\int_{J\cap(-\infty,t]}\phi_{\omega}(w-a)\,dw}{\displaystyle\int_{J}\phi_{\omega}(w-a)\,dw},\qquad\phi_{\omega}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\,\omega}\exp\left(-\frac{x^{2}}{2\omega^{2}}\right). All integrals use the entire section, including every interval component. Endpoints or isolated points do not change these integrals.

has conditional coverage 1−α1-\alpha for θ\theta. Both guarantees also hold conditional on ZZ for almost every selected zz.

Corollary 1 (Unique finite equal-tail interval endpoints).

Under Theorem 2, almost surely on EγretE_{\gamma}^{\rm ret} the confidence set is a closed interval [L,U][L,U] with unique finite endpoints solving

FL,ω𝒯γ,λret​(Z)​(T)=1−α/2,FU,ω𝒯γ,λret​(Z)​(T)=α/2.F^{\mathcal{T}_{\gamma,\lambda}^{\rm ret}(Z)}_{L,\omega}(T)=1-\alpha/2,\qquad F^{\mathcal{T}_{\gamma,\lambda}^{\rm ret}(Z)}_{U,\omega}(T)=\alpha/2. (24)

No bound on realized width or finite expected width is asserted.

The guarantee is finite-sample under the stated Gaussian model with known covariance. Small nn affects eligibility, the residual information d2d^{2} and the realized interval width, but does not add an asymptotic sample-size requirement to the conditional pivot.

Remark 2 (Ties and the unpruned limit).

All event and section identities above use exact growth priorities and collapse at pruning equality. They hold pointwise. If strict inequalities are replaced by weak inequalities for numerical integration, equality boundaries do not change the normal probabilities for almost every selected zz. At growth nodes, nonidentical ℓs​ℓs𝖳\ell_{s}\ell_{s}^{\mathsf{T}} give nonzero comparison polynomials in the full Gaussian outcome; finitely many possible labels imply a null union of their tie sets. The pruning boundary has at most two points for each zz because d>0d>0. Fubini’s theorem handles exceptional fibers on which a growth comparison is identically zero.

At λ=0\lambda=0, every selected gain is strictly positive almost surely under Assumption 1, by the same finite-label argument. The entire grown tree is then retained, and the unpruned inference is recovered almost surely. Exact ties at individual outcomes remain governed by the stated collapse convention.

Corollary 2 (A prespecified node address and availability).

Fix a node address before observing YY, and let 𝒱\mathcal{V} be the event that it is an internal node of the final pruned tree. If ℙ⁡(𝒱∣𝒟)>0\mathbb{P}(\mathcal{V}\mid\mathcal{D})>0, the interval for its selected target has coverage 1−α1-\alpha conditional on (𝒱,𝒟)(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{D}).

This is an individual-node guarantee. Without further adjustment, selecting the reported address by its smallest pp-value, largest estimate, or narrowest interval adds a selection event. Multiple-node simultaneous coverage is not supplied by this corollary. A collapsed node is unavailable for this split-specific inference; failure to retain a split does not establish homogeneous treatment effects.

4.5 Equivalence with full-tree conditioning

Lemma 3 (Canonical final tree on a retained section).

Under the growth and pruning assumptions, for every zz and t∈𝒯γ,λret​(z)t\in\mathcal{T}_{\gamma,\lambda}^{\rm ret}(z),

H^​(yz​(t))=Hγ​(z),P^λ​(yz​(t))=Pγ​(z).\widehat{H}(y_{z}(t))=H_{\gamma}(z),\qquad\widehat{P}_{\lambda}(y_{z}(t))=P_{\gamma}(z). (25)

Assume 3 and 4. Fix a complete labeled final tree PP containing γ\gamma as an internal path. Let

EP={P^λ(Y)=P},𝒜Pγ={z∈η⟂:Pγ(z)=P}.E_{P}=\{\widehat{P}_{\lambda}(Y)=P\},\qquad\mathcal{A}_{P}^{\gamma}=\{z\in\eta^{\perp}:P_{\gamma}(z)=P\}.

Then

EP=Eγret∩{Z∈𝒜Pγ}.\boxed{\quad E_{P}=E_{\gamma}^{\rm ret}\cap\{Z\in\mathcal{A}_{P}^{\gamma}\}.\quad} (26)

EH,P={H^(Y)=H,P^λ(Y)=P},𝒜H,Pγ={z:Hγ(z)=H,Pγ(z)=P}.E_{H,P}=\{\widehat{H}(Y)=H,\ \widehat{P}_{\lambda}(Y)=P\},\qquad\mathcal{A}_{H,P}^{\gamma}=\{z:H_{\gamma}(z)=H,\ P_{\gamma}(z)=P\}.

EH,P=Eγret∩{Z∈𝒜H,Pγ}.E_{H,P}=E_{\gamma}^{\rm ret}\cap\{Z\in\mathcal{A}_{H,P}^{\gamma}\}. (27)

All sets in these factorizations are measurable. Thus, for K=PK=P or K=(H,P)K=(H,P), the full-event section satisfies, for every zz,

𝒯K​(z):={t:yz​(t)∈EK}={𝒯γ,λret​(z),z∈𝒜Kγ,∅,z∉𝒜Kγ.\mathcal{T}_{K}(z):=\{t:y_{z}(t)\in E_{K}\}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{T}_{\gamma,\lambda}^{\rm ret}(z),&z\in\mathcal{A}_{K}^{\gamma},\\ \varnothing,&z\notin\mathcal{A}_{K}^{\gamma}.\end{cases} (28)

In particular, at every compatible observed y∈EKy\in E_{K} and z=y−c​η𝖳​yz=y-c\eta^{\mathsf{T}}y,

𝒯K​(z)=𝒯γ,λret​(z).\mathcal{T}_{K}(z)=\mathcal{T}_{\gamma,\lambda}^{\rm ret}(z). (29)

If Assumption 1 also holds and the relevant event has positive probability, the retained-path pivot, test, and confidence interval are exact conditional on the complete final tree alone, or on the pair of complete grown and final trees. At the observed compatible section they coincide with inference computed directly from those full events.

Remark 3 (What is, and is not, being equated).

The comparison is between growth plus survival of the target path and the complete final-tree event. Growth-only conditioning omits the pruning gate and generally gives different inference. Equality is asserted at compatible sections; a full-tree section is empty at an incompatible zz even when the retained-path section is nonempty.

Off-path quantities are not absent from the procedure: δγ​(z)\delta_{\gamma}(z) uses hanging-subtree pruning values. They can be calculated once after ZZ is fixed and add no further tt-dependent tree choices on the retained section. Ancestor competitors need not be orthogonal to the target, so all ancestor growth comparisons remain in (11). No independence between the target and the off-path tree after selection is asserted.

The equality yields a computational reduction in section construction. It does not make intervals shorter than their complete-tree-conditioned counterparts, which are identical, and pruning does not guarantee useful interval width.

Remark 4 (A simultaneous reporting option).

At one prespecified penalty λ\lambda, fix a complete final tree PP of positive selection probability and put K=|I⁡(P)|K=|I(P)|. Under the assumptions of Theorem 3, testing its projection nulls H0,v:ηv𝖳​μ=0H_{0,v}:\eta_{v}^{\mathsf{T}}\mu=0 at level α/K\alpha/K controls the familywise error probability conditional on (EP,𝒟)(E_{P},\mathcal{D}) at at most α\alpha. Likewise, intervals of individual level 1−α/K1-\alpha/K cover all KK selected targets jointly with conditional probability at least 1−α1-\alpha. If K=0K=0, no tests or intervals are reported. These conclusions follow by the union bound after conditioning on PP, where KK and the null indices are fixed; the target-specific orthogonal components need not coincide. This is a within-tree option, not a simultaneous guarantee across penalties or variance shapes. The simulations distinguish unadjusted α=0.05\alpha=0.05 per retained node from Bonferroni-adjusted tree-level rejection. Reported interval widths use nominal 95% individual intervals; widths of simultaneous intervals are not evaluated. A justification is provided in Section A.12 of Appendix A.

The present theory allows unequal known arm variances and, more generally, a known positive diagonal shape, but requires known scale and a penalty fixed before observing the outcomes. Appendix B gives an additive fixed-family extension, including certain fixed leaf-count constraints (Proposition B.3), and counterexamples showing why neither arbitrary pruning nor omission of target survival is covered automatically. Cross-validated or manually outcome-selected penalties, different pruning risks, outcome-selected bases, and variance substitution require additional arguments. The causal interpretation remains conditional on Assumption 2; the Gaussian projection guarantee alone is not population subgroup-average-effect inference.

5 Simulation

We investigate calibration after growing and pruning an interaction tree, the additional correction required by pruning, and the practical consequences of reusing a small trial for discovery and inference. The experiments also compare a same-rule honest procedure, examine the upper tail of interval widths, and assess substitution of an estimated common variance scale.

5.1 Data-generating mechanism

For each participant i=1,…,ni=1,\ldots,n, we independently generate

Xi​j​∼iid​Unif⁡(−1,1),j=1,…,5,Ai∼Bernoulli⁡(1/2),εi∼N⁡(0,1),X_{ij}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}\operatorname{Unif}(-1,1),\quad j=1,\ldots,5,\qquad A_{i}\sim\operatorname{Bernoulli}(1/2),\qquad\varepsilon_{i}\sim N(0,1),

with XiX_{i}, AiA_{i} and εi\varepsilon_{i} mutually independent, and set

Yi=m0​(Xi)+Ai​τ​(Xi)+1+(ρ−1)​Ai​εi,m0​(x)=2​x3+x4−x5.Y_{i}=m_{0}(X_{i})+A_{i}\tau(X_{i})+\sqrt{1+(\rho-1)A_{i}}\,\varepsilon_{i},\qquad m_{0}(x)=2x_{3}+x_{4}-x_{5}. (30)

Thus the control and treatment error variances are 11 and ρ\rho, respectively. We use n∈{100,200,400,800}n\in\{100,200,400,800\} and ρ∈{1/4,1,4}\rho\in\{1/4,1,4\}. The common reference basis is b⁡(x)=(1,x1,…,x5)𝖳b(x)=(1,x_{1},\ldots,x_{5})^{\mathsf{T}}, of dimension q=6q=6. The prognosis m0m_{0} lies in its span and is annihilated by every eligible interaction contrast; this design evaluates selection adjustment under correct prognostic specification, rather than sensitivity to prognostic misspecification.

We adapt the three-level mean-tree construction of Neufeld et al. (2022, Section 5.1) to treatment-effect heterogeneity:

τ(x)=0.5+γ𝟏{x1≤0}[1+a𝟏{x2>0}+𝟏{x2x3>0}].\tau(x)=0.5+\gamma\mathbf{1}\{x_{1}\leq 0\}\left[1+a\mathbf{1}\{x_{2}>0\}+\mathbf{1}\{x_{2}x_{3}>0\}\right]. (31)

There are five parameter settings,

(γ,a)∈{(0,1),(0.5,1),(1,1),(2,1),(1,0.5)}.(\gamma,a)\in\{(0,1),(0.5,1),(1,1),(2,1),(1,0.5)\}.

At γ=0\gamma=0, the CATE is the constant 0.50.5 and every interaction projection target is zero. This is a null of no mean-effect modification, compatible with unequal arm variances. The value of aa is then immaterial, so this setting is generated only once. Positive γ\gamma changes the amplitude of the three-level structure; a=0.5a=0.5 weakens the intermediate split relative to its descendants. Changing aa also changes the root contrast. A reference representation splits first on X1X_{1}, then on X2X_{2} within X1≤0X_{1}\leq 0, and on X3X_{3} in both resulting children. This representation need not be unique. All non-null settings have a depth-three structure, so maximum depths one and two restrict how much of it can be represented.

5.2 Tree construction and comparison procedures

At each reached parent, candidate generation enumerates every midpoint between distinct adjacent observed values of each covariate in that parent. The true cut point zero is not added to the search. Fixed feature and cut-point priorities resolve ties. Each growing split must have at least eight observations in every treatment-by-child cell and an identifiable weighted interaction. Numerical eligibility thresholds and representative-candidate reductions are specified in Section B.9 of Appendix B. All nodes use the common basis and the known variance shape Vi​i=1+(ρ−1)​AiV_{ii}=1+(\rho-1)A_{i}. Growth has no outcome-dependent stopping. We consider maximum depths D=1,2,3D=1,2,3, with root depth zero, and fixed additive subtree penalties λ=0,4,8\lambda=0,4,8, collapsing at equality. Depth DD permits at most DD splits along a path; it does not force that depth to be reached. We grow to depth three once, take each unpruned depth prefix, and apply pruning separately to that prefix. Since the true common scale is σ=1\sigma=1, the numerical penalties equal their variance-standardized values.

The four procedures differ as follows.

  1. (i)

    Naive uses the full-data grown and pruned tree and an ordinary known-variance Gaussian reference distribution, without selection adjustment.

  2. (ii)

    Growth-only uses the same tree and targets, conditions on the complete ancestral growth path, and omits the pruning-survival constraint.

  3. (iii)

    Selective adds the pruning-survival constraint to the growth event, using the procedure of Section 3.

  4. (iv)

    Honest randomly divides the trial into equal training and holdout samples. The training sample grows and prunes a GLS tree with the same basis, candidate-generation policy, minimum-cell rule and numerical penalty. Its learned thresholds are applied unchanged to the independent holdout sample, where ordinary GLS inference is performed. This implements the sample-separation principle of Athey and Imbens (2016), rather than reproducing a different causal-tree splitting objective.

Honest inference requires at least one holdout observation in each treatment-by-child cell, at least q+4=10q+4=10 holdout observations in the parent, and an identifiable interaction. The first three procedures share the full-data survivor set, GLS estimates and targets. Honest inference has its own learned tree, eligibility and holdout-design target. Its error-rate denominator therefore generally differs from theirs.

These rules impose concrete feasibility limits. A growing parent needs at least 32 observations, and a path with three internal splits needs at least 4×16=644\times 16=64. Consequently, the honest training sample of 50 at n=100n=100 cannot produce a third-stage split, although shallower splits can be inferred. This is a property of the specified 50:50, minimum-eight comparator. The comparison does not assert an advantage over every possible honest design.

The principal experiment uses the true covariance. An additional module replaces only the common reference scale by an estimate, retaining the same known variance ratio and numerical penalty. Its construction and results are reported in Section 5.7.

5.3 Performance measures and Monte Carlo design

For each sample size, we generate 5,000 independent constant-effect trials and 1,000 independent trials for each of the four non-null settings: 36,000 independent base trials overall. Within a base trial, the covariates, allocation, unit Gaussian errors and honest partition are shared across the three variance ratios, producing 108,000 correlated outcome versions. Each version is reused across the three depth limits and three penalties. Outcome versions, nodes and derived settings are not independent Monte Carlo replications. A separate 480-trial pilot checked computation and retention before the penalties, replication counts and endpoint subset were frozen; pilot results are not pooled with the main experiment.

Every potential node address is recorded, including ungrown, pruned and holdout-ineligible positions. Inference availability is the probability that at least one target can be computed, using all trials, including empty trees. Splitwise rejection at p<0.05p<0.05 and coverage condition on successfully computed eligible retained splits. The denominator is the total number of such splits, not the number of participants or trials, and is reported separately for the full-data and honest procedures. Coverage is evaluated against the actual θv=ηv𝖳​μ\theta_{v}=\eta_{v}^{\mathsf{T}}\mu for each selected analysis design. The piecewise CATE values in (31) are not substituted for these projections. Rejection is a false-positive rate (FPR) at γ=0\gamma=0; under heterogeneity it describes discovery among selected targets, rather than power for a common fixed parameter.

To assess recovery, we adapt the split-matching strategy of Neufeld et al. (2022, Section 5.4). Both procedures are evaluated on the same fixed set of 4,096 independently generated covariate vectors. Within each reference parent, its binary child labels are compared with an estimated split’s three labels: left child, right child, or outside the estimated parent. A reference split is matched to the retained estimated split with largest adjusted Rand index (ARI); ARI greater than 0.750.75 defines recovery. Deterministic traversal order resolves ties, and multiple reference splits may match one estimated split. We report recovery and the joint event of recovery, successful inference and rejection, each over all trials. This is local partition matching, not recovery of an entire hierarchical tree. In particular, a shallow estimated split can agree with a deeper reference split when labels are restricted to the reference parent. Actual growth depth is assessed separately.

All eligible trials evaluate the true-target pivot and its coverage decision. Confidence-interval endpoints and widths are computed only for the prespecified trial indices 1–500 in each sample-size/effect/ratio setting, without replacing unavailable intervals. We retain every computed width and summarize its count, median, 90th percentile and extremes. Width groups with fewer than 30 intervals are flagged. Fixed-address and trial-wise events use Wilson Monte Carlo intervals. Pooled depth and tree rates use ratio estimates with trial-cluster Monte Carlo standard errors (MCSEs), retaining trials with no available splits. Paired differences are used for the same-target full-data procedures and for known versus estimated scale within a procedure. General Honest comparisons concern different selected populations and targets. Reported Monte Carlo intervals are pointwise across the correlated reporting grid.

Individual tests are distinguished from the probability of any rejection in a tree. The latter uses all trials, including empty trees. We also apply Bonferroni at 0.05/K0.05/K, where KK is the method’s retained split count, including holdout-ineligible honest splits, and make no rejection for an empty tree. These comparisons are within fixed configurations, with no selection of a penalty from the main outcomes.

Independent numerical checks compared candidate scores and coefficients with direct weighted QR and GLS calculations, checked selection sections against actual regrowth and pruning, and verified the known/estimated-scale target identities. All main records passed post-run completeness and pairing checks; there were no inference or endpoint failures. Extreme intervals were reconstructed and their endpoints checked independently at 100-decimal precision. The accompanying code specifies the study settings, seeds and commands needed to regenerate the results.

5.4 Calibration and the need to adjust for pruning

Figure 1 compares the three growth limits at λ=4\lambda=4, and Table 1 gives both methods’ split counts and the stronger-pruning comparison at ρ=1\rho=1, D=3D=3. In the constant-effect model at D=3D=3, λ=4\lambda=4, selective pooled FPRs across sample sizes and variance ratios ranged from 4.78%4.78\% to 5.38%5.38\%, with trial-cluster MCSEs of 0.150.15–0.260.26 percentage points. On the same retained full-data targets, naive FPRs ranged from 94.94%94.94\% to 98.79%98.79\%. Under the four non-null settings, selective coverage at D=3D=3, λ=4\lambda=4 ranged from 94.29%94.29\% to 95.88%95.88\%, with MCSEs of 0.270.27–0.570.57 percentage points. These results support calibration in the stated Gaussian experiment; they are not a simultaneous empirical guarantee for every cell.

The incremental pruning correction is clearest at the stronger penalty. For n=100n=100, ρ=1\rho=1, D=3D=3 and λ=8\lambda=8, growth-only inference rejected 14.57%14.57\% of the 1,270 retained full-data targets, compared with 5.75%5.75\% for selective inference. Their paired difference was −8.82-8.82 percentage points (MCSE 1.001.00). At n=800n=800, the corresponding rates were 8.37%8.37\% and 4.81%4.81\% on 6,096 targets, with paired difference −3.56-3.56 points (MCSE 0.310.31). The grown tree, pruned survivor set and targets are identical within each comparison, isolating the consequence of omitting pruning survival. At λ=4\lambda=4 the additional effect is smaller in some settings; at λ=0\lambda=0, growth-only and selective calculations agree, as required.

Strong pruning also makes some conditional populations sparse. At n=100n=100, ρ=1\rho=1, D=3D=3 and λ=8\lambda=8, Honest inference had 343 computed targets and only 29 endpoint intervals in the fixed subset. Deep fixed-address cells can be smaller still. Such groups remain in the summaries, with their counts and uncertainty, and are not used to claim precise calibration or stable width quantiles.

Pruning does not itself provide tree-wide multiplicity control. For the selective procedure at n=800n=800, ρ=1\rho=1, D=3D=3, λ=4\lambda=4, the individual pooled FPR was 4.88%4.88\%, while the probability of at least one rejection was 18.96%18.96\%. Bonferroni reduced the latter to 4.24%4.24\%. All 5,000 trials, including empty trees, enter these tree-level probabilities.

5.5 Honest comparison: availability and reference-split recovery

The larger full-data split count describes more opportunities for inference, not necessarily successful detection of heterogeneity. For example, at γ=0\gamma=0, n=100n=100, ρ=1\rho=1, D=3D=3, λ=4\lambda=4, the full-data procedures assessed 7,854 splits and Honest assessed 2,366, over the same 5,000 base trials. The probabilities of any eligible inference were 85.68%85.68\% and 47.16%47.16\%, respectively. Every target is null in this setting, so availability alone is not a discovery advantage.

With genuine heterogeneity, using all outcomes for learning improved reference-partition matching in the small trial. At (γ,a)=(1,1)(\gamma,a)=(1,1), ρ=1\rho=1, D=3D=3, λ=4\lambda=4 and n=100n=100, the reference-root recovery rates were 76.5%76.5\% for the full-data tree and 53.4%53.4\% for Honest. The joint probabilities of recovery, inference and rejection were 51.1%51.1\% and 45.0%45.0\%; their MCSEs were 1.581.58 and 1.571.57 percentage points. These events use all 1,000 trials as denominator. Any eligible inference was available in 100%100\% and 94.7%94.7\% of these trials, respectively. Figure 2 shows how reference-root matching and joint discovery vary with signal amplitude.

Improved recovery did not imply uniformly improved discovery. At n=400n=400 and 800800 in the same setting, recovery-and-rejection probabilities were 89.9%89.9\% and 95.6%95.6\% for Selective, versus 92.9%92.9\% and 98.5%98.5\% for Honest. Thus learning a reference partition more often and obtaining significant evidence after conditioning are distinct objectives. The procedures’ interval widths and general discovery rates also refer to their own selected targets, not a paired comparison of one invariant treatment-effect contrast. Actual third-stage honest splits were absent at n=100n=100, as required by the training-size constraint; local ARI matches to deep reference splits do not change this structural fact.

5.6 Interval widths and their limitations

Table 2 distinguishes actual split stage from maximum growth depth and separates inferential counts from endpoint counts. For (γ,a)=(1,1)(\gamma,a)=(1,1), ρ=1\rho=1, D=3D=3 and λ=4\lambda=4, the root median widths at n=100n=100 were 2.2162.216 for Selective and 2.4432.443 for Honest, based on 500 and 478 intervals. Their 90th percentiles were 4.2254.225 and 2.7092.709. At n=800n=800, the root medians were 0.5620.562 and 0.7920.792, but the 90th percentiles were 1.0871.087 and 0.7990.799. A shorter median therefore coexisted with a longer upper tail.

Deep selective intervals were substantially wider. At n=400n=400 in the same setting, third-stage medians were 8.1658.165 and 2.2672.267, and 90th percentiles were 47.19547.195 and 2.9242.924, based on 1,408 and 754 intervals. These are descriptive comparisons of each procedure’s own targets and survivor population. Pooling all stages changes the composition further: additional deep targets can increase the pooled width summary even while root intervals shorten with nn. Likewise, an alternative-model pooled rejection rate can fall as more weak targets become available; it is not a common-target power curve.

Figure 3 retains the depth-specific upper-tail behavior. Across the fixed endpoint subsets, the largest selective width with known scale was approximately 3.78×1063.78\times 10^{6}, at n=400n=400, γ=0\gamma=0, ρ=1/4\rho=1/4, D=3D=3, λ=4\lambda=4. The estimated-scale version of the same split had width approximately 3.83×1063.83\times 10^{6}. Regenerating the trial, refitting its selection section and checking the endpoints at high precision supported these values; they were not removed or capped. Correct coverage does not ensure useful precision. On the target-score line, ancestor comparisons can impose finite outer boundaries in addition to the central exclusions from growth and pruning (Corollary B.1); this geometry explains a source of inversion sensitivity without diagnosing every long interval or asserting monotonicity in depth.

5.7 Substituting an estimated common scale

The additional module keeps the variance ratio ρ\rho known and estimates only the common scale. Regressing control outcomes on the prespecified basis gives

σ^2=RSS0n0−rank⁡(B0),\widehat{\sigma}^{2}=\frac{\RSS_{0}}{n_{0}-\operatorname{rank}(B_{0})}, (32)

where B0B_{0} is the control-group basis matrix. For the full-data procedures this uses all controls; Honest uses training controls only and keeps the estimate fixed during holdout inference. Control outcomes contain no treatment-effect heterogeneity, and their prognosis is correctly specified here. The estimate need not be independent of the learned tree. We substitute σ^\widehat{\sigma} only in the truncated-normal reference distribution, leaving VV, the raw numerical λ\lambda, the tree and the target unchanged. The comparison covers γ=0\gamma=0 and (γ,a)=(1,1)(\gamma,a)=(1,1), all sample sizes, ratios and depth limits, at λ=4\lambda=4. It does not estimate both arm variances or establish exactness with unknown covariance.

For Selective at D=3D=3, the largest reduction in coverage relative to known scale was 0.360.36 percentage points under the constant effect and 0.460.46 points under (γ,a)=(1,1)(\gamma,a)=(1,1). Table 3 reports method-specific counts and paired changes, and Figure 4 separates actual split stages. At n=100n=100, ρ=1\rho=1, (γ,a)=(1,1)(\gamma,a)=(1,1), Selective coverage changed from 95.10%95.10\% to 94.70%94.70\% on the same 2,206 targets. Honest coverage changed from 95.26%95.26\% to 93.26%93.26\% on its own 949 targets, a paired difference of −2.00-2.00 percentage points (MCSE 0.560.56). At ρ=4\rho=4, the honest paired change was −2.50-2.50 points (MCSE 0.610.61) on 801 targets. These results indicate limited sensitivity for the specified Selective scale estimator in this experiment and a detectable small-sample effect of scale substitution for Honest. They remain empirical observations under known variance shape and correct prognosis, separate from the finite-sample known-covariance guarantee.

6 Real-data application: ACTG 175

6.1 Scientific question and public analysis sample

ACTG 175 compared four nucleoside regimens in adults with HIV infection (Hammer et al., 1996). We examine the historical comparison of zidovudine (ZDV) plus didanosine (ddI) with ZDV plus zalcitabine (zal, also denoted ddC). The scientific question is whether combinations of baseline immune status, age, and prior-treatment history describe an adjusted interaction in early immunologic response. We use the CD4 count at 20±520\pm 5 weeks on its original scale, in cells per cubic millimeter. This quantitative response differs from the original trial’s primary endpoint combining CD4 decline, AIDS progression, and death. The companion biomarker investigation supplies the context for early immune response (Katzenstein et al., 1996). The same two combination regimens and 20-week response were used by Fan et al. (2017, Section 4); our search rule, nuisance basis, and projection targets are those of the present method.

The public ACTG175 file in speff2trial version 1.0.5 contains 2139 participants and 27 variables (Juraska et al., 2022). Restricting arms to 1 and 2 gives 522 ZDV+ddI and 524 ZDV+zal assignments, respectively, for n=1046n=1046. We set A=1A=1 for ZDV+ddI and A=0A=0 for ZDV+zal. All selected baseline variables and 20-week responses are recorded in this public subset. The original trial reported 2467 participants; Huang and Chan (2020, Section 5.2) describe the 2139 records as remaining after exclusion of missing or unrecorded relevant information, without identifying the complete exclusion rule. We therefore do not interpret public-file completeness as complete original-trial follow-up or claim to reproduce the original intention-to-treat analysis. Three records have baseline CD4 equal to zero and are retained as supplied; the inspected dictionary does not identify zero as a missing-value code. No response transformation, outcome imputation, or outlier deletion is used.

6.2 Maximum-depth-three unpruned analysis

The main display is an unpruned interaction tree with maximum depth three, root depth zero, and dimensionless penalty λ~=0\widetilde{\lambda}=0. We report every eligible grown internal split. Maximum depth is an upper bound: a region stops earlier when its design has no eligible candidate. With zero penalty, growth-only and pruning-aware calculations coincide for the observed trees, so the main comparison has three distinct procedures: Naive, Selective, and Honest. Here Selective denotes the common growth-adjusted and pruning-aware result, rather than two separate empirical competitors. The additional contribution of correcting positive-penalty pruning is examined in the theoretical results and controlled simulations; positive-penalty application calculations are summarized below as exploratory references.

Earlier exploration of these public data had already included outcome-distribution diagnostics, restricted-grid trees and several fixed penalties. The present expansion to all adjacent-observation cut points was adopted after those results had been inspected. Before this rerun, we retained the original-scale response, common basis, maximum depth, minimum-cell rule, saved Honest partition and unpruned main display, and fixed the expanded candidate policy and all four positive-penalty references. These choices are not an outcome-unseen analysis plan. Neither candidate-policy selection nor selection of the response scale or main display is included in the growth-conditioning event, and no additional adjustment for these exploratory choices is claimed.

The common basis contains an intercept, baseline CD4, baseline CD8, age, weight, Karnofsky score, recorded sex, symptom indicator, prior antiretroviral days, and two indicators for the three-level prior-treatment stratum. Nonconstant columns are centered and scaled using the 1046 baseline records, preserving the column space. Every candidate uses Cs=[BR,AR,hs]C_{s}=[B_{R},A_{R},h_{s}] as in (3); rank deficiency is allowed, but the interaction coefficient must be identifiable. The six search variables, in fixed priority order, are baseline CD4, baseline CD8, age, prior-treatment days, prior experience, and symptoms. Within each reached parent, every midpoint between distinct adjacent observed values of a continuous search variable is considered; the binary variables have threshold 0.50.5. The full-data tree constructs candidates from its parent observations, whereas Honest constructs its thresholds from training covariates alone and applies those same numerical thresholds to holdout participants. Each treatment-by-child cell must contain at least 20 participants during growth. Exact duplicate or complementary child partitions use their first fixed-priority representative. Post-randomization variables are excluded.

The variances are unknown. Groupwise regressions on the fixed basis give sa2=RSSa/{na−rank⁡(Ba)}s_{a}^{2}=\RSS_{a}/\{n_{a}-\operatorname{rank}(B_{a})\}. The full-data calculations freeze V^i​i=sAi2\widehat{V}_{ii}=s_{A_{i}}^{2} and σ=1\sigma=1 for growth and inference, with estimated standard deviations 104.8919104.8919 and 132.0497132.0497 for ZDV+zal and ZDV+ddI, respectively. Variances are not re-estimated within selected leaves. Honest uses one saved 523/523 split, generated from sorted participant IDs with seed 20261028: training arm counts are 263/260 and holdout counts are 261/262, ordered as ZDV+zal/ZDV+ddI. Its two variance pilots use training outcomes alone, giving standard deviations 101.2552101.2552 and 146.5730146.5730, and are frozen for both training growth and holdout inference. A held-out contrast requires at least 15 observations in its parent, at least one in each treatment-by-child cell, and an identifiable interaction coefficient. Figure 5 reports the complete split rules and arm counts.

6.3 Unpruned results and positive-penalty reference analyses

At λ=0\lambda=0, all 6 full-data grown splits and all 4 Honest training splits remain. Their distinct eligible root-candidate counts are 1,443 and 828, respectively. Of the training-selected Honest splits, 4 support inference in their holdout regions. Figure 5 gives both unpruned trees, and Table 4 reports every primary-display record: 6 Naive, 6 Selective and 4 Honest. Growth-only and pruning-aware calculations have identical probabilities, intervals and pp-values at zero penalty and are displayed once as Selective.

The full-data root rule is Age≤39.5\mathrm{Age}\leq 39.5, with GLS interaction estimate −65.50-65.50. Its naive nominal 95% interval is [−97.97,−33.04][-97.97,-33.04] (p<0.001p<0.001), compared with the Selective interval [−92.12,21.67][-92.12,21.67] (p=0.651p=0.651). Across the full-data tree, 5 of 6 Naive intervals and 1 of 6 Selective intervals exclude zero. These changes concern nominal evidence after the observed search, not demonstrated false positives or known clinical truth. The sole Selective exclusion is at node R, with rule CD40≤452.5\mathrm{CD4}_{0}\leq 452.5 in that node’s parent, estimate −103.50-103.50 and interval [−174.06,−8.05][-174.06,-8.05] (p=0.036p=0.036).

The Honest root rule is Age≤39.5\mathrm{Age}\leq 39.5, geometrically agreeing with the full-data root. Its holdout-design estimate is −38.87-38.87, with interval [−86.25,8.52][-86.25,8.52] (p=0.108p=0.108). One of the 4 available Honest intervals excludes zero. The Honest exclusion occurs at node LL, with rule CD40≤342.5\mathrm{CD4}_{0}\leq 342.5, holdout estimate −69.40-69.40 and interval [−131.32,−7.49][-131.32,-7.49] (p=0.028p=0.028). This is a different rule and target from the full-data nominal exclusion.

The full-data Selective and Honest median widths are 279.38279.38 and 128.30128.30, and their maxima are 1518.141518.14 and 164.23164.23, respectively. The rules, working weights and analysis designs can differ, so these are descriptive procedural comparisons rather than efficiencies for a common clinical parameter. Figure 6 displays every endpoint without clipping.

For fixed positive penalties λ=1,2,3,4\lambda=1,2,3,4, the numbers of retained full-data splits are 6, 6, 5, 4, and the corresponding Honest training counts are 4, 4, 4, 3. At λ=3\lambda=3 and 44, the retained full-data R contrast keeps its estimate of −103.50-103.50, but its pruning-aware pp-values become 0.0980.098 and 0.1800.180; growth-only inference remains at p=0.036p=0.036. Thus no Selective interval excludes zero at these two penalties. Honest retains its LL exclusion through penalty three, whereas penalty four removes that split. All reference results are retained in the reproducibility files. Positive penalties may alter the truncation section even when the retained tree is unchanged. The largest Selective reference width is 1518.141518.14. These are exploratory reference calculations; no penalty is selected from its nominal pp-value.

6.4 Interpretation and limits

All application intervals and pp-values are nominal working-model calculations. Treating estimated group variances as fixed defines the computation but does not satisfy Assumption 1. Raw CD4 is a nonnegative count response. Groupwise residual diagnostics show right-tail departures, particularly in the ZDV+zal reference group; mean-model lack of fit and treatment-effect variation can also contribute to these residual patterns. Neither the raw-scale choice nor the sample size establishes a conditional Gaussian law. Training-only variance estimation prevents holdout leakage into selection but does not supply a known-true-variance guarantee for Honest. Algebraic agreement of compatible path and full-tree sections is not evidence of exact clinical coverage under these departures.

The target ηs𝖳​μ\eta_{s}^{\mathsf{T}}\mu is a finite-design GLS interaction specific to its selected split, basis, allocation, and working variance ratio. Its weighted-CATE interpretation additionally requires causal identification in this analyzed subset and a correct prognosis under the new reference regimen, ZDV+zal. The unknown public-file inclusion rule prevents us from deriving these conditions from original randomization alone. Facility identifiers are absent, limiting assessment of residual dependence. Full-data and Honest estimates can concern different rules and holdout-design targets, so their widths are not paired efficiencies for one invariant clinical parameter. All displayed intervals are individual 95% intervals, with no demonstrated tree-wide familywise guarantee. This single observed dataset estimates neither coverage nor false-positive rates. The exploratory comparisons and nominal exclusions of zero do not establish treatment recommendations.

7 Discussion

We developed selective inference for pruned, covariate-adjusted interaction trees with known unequal outcome variances. Building on the Tree-Values framework (Neufeld et al., 2022), we established common-basis GLS orthogonality for residualized treatment interactions. Under additive fixed-penalty pruning, this geometry reduces retention of a selected path to its growth constraints and one quadratic pruning-survival inequality, yielding exact finite-sample conditional tests and confidence intervals under the stated Gaussian model. We also showed that retained-path and complete-tree conditioning give identical inference on compatible sections. This factorization simplifies computation while preserving the complete-tree-conditioned intervals.

The theory identifies a finite-design GLS target that remains unchanged when a split survives pruning. Under causal identification and a correct reference prognosis, this target is a signed weighted contrast of conditional average treatment effects. Its weights depend on allocation, covariates and variance shape, so it generally differs from an ordinary subgroup-average treatment-effect contrast. This distinction connects the inferential guarantee to the specific interaction being estimated and clarifies the additional assumptions needed for a causal interpretation.

Simulations at n=100,200,400,800n=100,200,400,800, with maximum depths one to three and all adjacent-observation candidate midpoints, demonstrated the practical importance of correcting both growth and pruning. Known-variance results supported nominal calibration. For example, at n=100n=100, ρ=1\rho=1, D=3D=3 and λ=8\lambda=8 under a constant effect, growth-only inference rejected 14.57%14.57\% of retained contrasts, compared with 5.75%5.75\% after pruning correction on the same targets (Section 5.4). Full-data learning improved reference-split recovery in some small-sample settings, although subsequent discovery probabilities were not uniformly higher. Root-level median intervals could be shorter than Honest intervals, while deeper intervals and upper tails were substantially wider. These comparisons describe each procedure’s selected targets and populations.

The Honest comparison highlights the value of preserving data for exploration in small samples. Dividing observations between training and inference reduces the information available to each task, and local minimum-cell requirements can prevent further refinement. In ACTG 175, requiring 20 observations in each treatment-by-child cell requires at least 40 in each treatment arm of a parent. The Honest training region LR contained 46 and 38 observations and could not be split further. The full-data and Honest trees had six and four internal splits, respectively (Figure 5). Full-data exploration can therefore preserve opportunities for finer partitioning, while the wide nominal Selective intervals in Figure 6 show the limits to the precision of the resulting inference.

Honest results also depend on the particular training/holdout assignment, which can change the eligible candidates, learned groups, inferential targets and intervals. This dependence can be a practical concern for analysts. A fixed seed makes one realization reproducible, but does not establish stability across alternative partitions; we did not quantify this sensitivity. The full-data procedure avoids this additional random partition, although its tree can still be sensitive to changes in the observed sample. The combination of richer exploration and selection adjustment is thus a practical advantage, with useful precision and stable subgroup discovery remaining separate objectives.

The exact guarantees require a conditional Gaussian model with known positive diagonal covariance and prespecified growth and pruning rules. They concern individual selected contrasts; simultaneous reporting requires an additional multiplicity adjustment. Our estimated-scale experiment retained a known variance ratio and showed modest changes in Selective coverage in the settings examined, without establishing unknown-variance validity. ACTG 175 uses estimated arm variances and has residual tail departures, unresolved public-subset inclusion and prior exploratory analysis choices. Its results remain nominal working-model illustrations. Developing valid theory for unknown arm-specific variances, and assessing robustness to prognosis misspecification and non-Gaussian outcomes, are central practical extensions.

Further work could improve how information is allocated between discovery and inference. Data thinning can construct independent components of each response while retaining the covariate design (Neufeld et al., 2024); data carving can use information remaining in the selection sample after conditioning (Fithian et al., 2014); and randomized selection offers another way to retain information for subsequent inference (Tian and Taylor, 2018). Incorporating these strategies into interaction-tree growth and pruning may enable more efficient estimation and inference. Their adaptation requires new selection laws and evaluation of estimation error, power and interval precision. Gaussian thinning itself relies on known covariance, so it does not resolve the unknown-variance problem. Establishing when these extensions improve performance in small samples is an important direction for future research.

Appendix A Proofs of the main results

A.1 Proof of Proposition 1

Proof.

At a terminal node the only admissible score is zero. At an internal node, collapsing gives zero; retaining gives its penalized gain plus the optimal scores in its two children. The maximum is precisely (6). If Vw<0V_{w}<0, every optimum collapses. If Vw=0V_{w}=0, collapsing has zero internal nodes, fewer than any retained alternative. If Vw>0V_{w}>0, every optimum retains ww and uses optimal subtrees in both children. By induction, the minimum-node choices in the children are unique, proving both optimality and uniqueness. One bottom-up pass computes the values and one top-down pass reconstructs the tree. ∎

A.4 Proof of Lemma 2

Proof.

Fix the design and a feasible labeled path γ\gamma ending at the target ⋆\star. Its contrast vectors, candidate rules, and node regions are then fixed. For Steps 1–4, fix z∈η⟂z\in\eta^{\perp} and t∈𝒯γgrow​(z)t\in\mathcal{T}_{\gamma}^{\rm grow}(z), and abbreviate y=yz​(t)=z+v​ty=y_{z}(t)=z+vt, since c=vc=v in (9). By the definition of the growth section, ordinary growth at yy selects every prescribed split along γ\gamma.

Step 1: invariance of every off-path candidate score. An off-path region reached in the canonical construction lies either in a child of the target or in a sibling branch leaving its ancestral path. In the latter case it is disjoint from the target’s parent. For every eligible candidate rr in any such region, Lemma 1 therefore gives

ℓr𝖳​v=vr𝖳​W​vdr=0.\ell_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}v=\frac{v_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}Wv}{d_{r}}=0.

Consequently, both its linear score and its squared split score agree at yy and zz:

ℓr𝖳​y=ℓr𝖳​z+t​ℓr𝖳​v=ℓr𝖳​z,Gr​(y)=Gr​(z).\ell_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}y=\ell_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}z+t\ell_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}v=\ell_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}z,\qquad G_{r}(y)=G_{r}(z).

This assertion concerns all candidates in the region, including candidates that are not ultimately selected. Thus every pairwise score comparison, with its exact equality status, is unchanged there.

Step 2: equality of the complete labeled grown trees. Compare ordinary growth at yy with the construction of Hγ​(z)H_{\gamma}(z), proceeding from the root down. Suppose the two constructions have reached the same region. Eligibility, the candidate set, and the stopping rule coincide, because Assumption 3 makes them functions only of the design and that region. If the node is on γ\gamma, ordinary growth chooses the prescribed split because tt belongs to the growth section; the canonical construction forces that same split. If the node is off the path, Step 1 shows that every candidate has the same score in the two constructions. Their fixed priorities therefore select the same winner, including at ties. In either case the chosen split labels and the resulting child regions coincide, or both constructions stop. Induction up to the finite maximum depth proves

H^​(yz​(t))=Hγ​(z).\widehat{H}(y_{z}(t))=H_{\gamma}(z).

The restriction to the growth section is essential: competing candidates at a path node can have scores that vary with tt, so the prescribed path need not be selected outside that section.

Step 3: invariance of all selected non-target scores. Consider an internal node w≠⋆w\neq\star of this common tree. If it is off the path, Step 1 already gives Gw​(y)=Gw​(z)G_{w}(y)=G_{w}(z). Otherwise, it is a prescribed ancestor of the target. Applying the nested-region identity of Lemma 1 to that ancestor and the target yields

ℓw𝖳​v=vw𝖳​W​vdw=0.\ell_{w}^{\mathsf{T}}v=\frac{v_{w}^{\mathsf{T}}Wv}{d_{w}}=0.

The same linear-score calculation as in Step 1 therefore gives Gw​(y)=Gw​(z)G_{w}(y)=G_{w}(z) for every selected non-target node. This does not assert invariance of competing candidates at ancestor nodes.

Step 4: the target score. For the target, ℓ=d​η\ell=d\eta and η𝖳​z=0\eta^{\mathsf{T}}z=0. The normalization in (3) gives

η𝖳​v=v𝖳​W​vd2=1.\eta^{\mathsf{T}}v=\frac{v^{\mathsf{T}}Wv}{d^{2}}=1.

It follows that

ℓ𝖳​yz​(t)=d​η𝖳​(z+v​t)=d​t,G⋆​(yz​(t))=d2​t2.\ell^{\mathsf{T}}y_{z}(t)=d\eta^{\mathsf{T}}(z+vt)=dt,\qquad G_{\star}(y_{z}(t))=d^{2}t^{2}.

Together with Steps 2 and 3, this proves all three identities in (12).

Step 5: measurability of the completion maps. The finite maximum depth and the finite candidate sets at every possible region give finitely many feasible labeled grown trees. Feasibility of γ\gamma ensures that its forced nodes respect the design-only eligibility and stopping rules independently of zz. For each fixed region and candidate, the loading ℓr\ell_{r} is fixed by the design, and Gr​(z)=(ℓr𝖳​z)2G_{r}(z)=(\ell_{r}^{\mathsf{T}}z)^{2} is a quadratic polynomial in zz. Hence each exact winning condition is a finite intersection of strict or weak polynomial inequalities, and is Borel measurable. For a fixed feasible tree HH, the event {z:Hγ​(z)=H}\{z:H_{\gamma}(z)=H\} is obtained by combining these off-path winning conditions with the forced path and the design-only stopping rules. It is therefore Borel. This proves measurability of HγH_{\gamma} on η⟂\eta^{\perp}.

On each such fixed HH, the pruning recursion in (6) forms continuation values by finitely many additions and maxima of continuous scores. Its decisions to retain or collapse an off-path node, including collapse at equality, are consequently Borel measurable. Joining these pruned hanging subtrees to the forced path proves measurability of PγP_{\gamma} as well. This argument applies to every z∈η⟂z\in\eta^{\perp}, even when its growth section is empty. It does not assert that the forced path survives ordinary pruning. All arguments above are deterministic; Gaussian sampling and a causal mean representation are not required. ∎
